concepts.name: Bindusara's Regnal Titles and Epithets
key_dimensions: Title 'Amitraghata' (Slayer of Enemies) in Greek sources vs. 'Bindusara' in Indian sources
Greek rendering as 'Amitrochates' or 'Allitrochades' — source-based confusion trap
Jain tradition calling him 'Sinhasenha' — cross-tradition discrepancy
UPSC trap: distinguishing which title appears in which foreign account (Strabo, Athenaeus)

concepts.name: Bindusara's Position in Mauryan Dynastic Succession
key_dimensions: Son of Chandragupta Maurya and father of Ashoka — dynastic continuity angle
Approximate regnal period (~297–272 BCE) and its contestation among historians
Puranic lists vs. Buddhist sources on Mauryan succession order
UPSC trap: confusing Bindusara's reign dates with Chandragupta's or Ashoka's

concepts.name: Bindusara's Diplomatic Relations with Hellenic World
key_dimensions: Exchange of letters with Antiochus I Soter (Seleucid king) — nature and content
Famous request for 'sweet wine, dried figs, and a sophist' — what Antiochus could/could not send
Ambassador Deimachus at Bindusara's court — comparison with Megasthenes at Chandragupta's court
UPSC trap: confusing Deimachus (Bindusara's era) with Megasthenes (Chandragupta's era)

concepts.name: Deimachus as Ambassador and His Literary Contribution
key_dimensions: Sent by Antiochus I to Bindusara's court — source: Strabo and Pliny
His account critiqued by Strabo for inaccuracies — reliability question
Comparison with Megasthenes' Indica as a source for Mauryan history
UPSC trap: Deimachus wrote about India but his work is lost — known only through fragments/criticism

concepts.name: Bindusara's Territorial Expansion and Military Campaigns
key_dimensions: Claim of conquering 'land between two seas' (Arabian Sea to Bay of Bengal) — Taranatha's account
Consolidation of Deccan territories inherited from Chandragupta
Extent of Mauryan Empire under Bindusara vs. under Chandragupta and Ashoka
UPSC trap: Ashoka is credited with Kalinga conquest, not Bindusara — territorial attribution errors

concepts.name: Bindusara's Religious Affiliations and Patronage
key_dimensions: Association with the Ajivika sect — primary religious leaning
Contrast with Chandragupta (Jainism) and Ashoka (Buddhism) — dynastic religious shift
Ajivikas as a heterodox sect: fatalistic philosophy (Niyati) and its political implications
UPSC trap: all three Mauryan rulers had different religious affiliations — frequently confused

concepts.name: Ajivikas Under Bindusara: Royal Patronage and Sect Characteristics
key_dimensions: Ajivika sect founded by Makkhali Gosala — doctrinal overview
Bindusara's patronage contrasted with Ashoka's later grant of caves to Ajivikas (Barabar caves)
Doctrine of absolute determinism (Niyati) distinguishing Ajivikas from Buddhists and Jains
UPSC trap: Barabar cave inscriptions are by Ashoka for Ajivikas, not Bindusara — attribution trap

concepts.name: Bindusara's Administrative Practices and Provincial Governance
key_dimensions: Appointment of Ashoka as Viceroy of Ujjain and Taxila — viceregal system continuity
Susima (eldest son) as Viceroy of Taxila — succession politics
Suppression of Taxila revolt — Ashoka's role and Bindusara's administrative response
UPSC trap: distinguishing which prince was posted where and under whose orders

concepts.name: Taxila Revolt During Bindusara's Reign
key_dimensions: Nature of revolt: against local officials, not against Mauryan authority per se
Ashoka's role in suppressing the revolt — first major political assignment
Sources: Divyavadana (Buddhist text) as primary reference
UPSC trap: revolt was not anti-Mauryan — a nuance often misrepresented in options

concepts.name: Succession Crisis After Bindusara: Ashoka vs. Susima
key_dimensions: Susima as designated heir vs. Ashoka's political rise — court intrigue
Role of minister Radhagupta (or Khallataka) in supporting Ashoka's claim
Buddhist sources (Mahavamsa, Divyavadana) on fratricidal war — historicity debate
UPSC trap: number of brothers killed (99 or fewer) varies across sources — factual trap

concepts.name: Primary Source Evidence for Bindusara: Classical and Indian
key_dimensions: Greek/Roman sources: Strabo, Athenaeus, Pliny — fragmentary and secondhand
Indian sources: Puranas (dynastic lists), Buddhist texts (Divyavadana, Mahavamsa)
Jain texts: Rajavalikatha mentioning Bindusara
UPSC trap: no inscriptional evidence directly from Bindusara — contrast with Ashoka's prolific epigraphy

concepts.name: Bindusara and the Brahmin Intellectual Tradition
key_dimensions: Association with Brahmin scholars — Chanakya's continued influence at court (debated)
Request for a 'sophist' from Antiochus — reflects intellectual curiosity and Greek parallel
Subandhu as minister mentioned in some accounts — court intellectual culture
UPSC trap: Chanakya's presence/death during Bindusara's reign is historically debated, not confirmed

concepts.name: Bindusara's Reign as a Period of Consolidation vs. Expansion
key_dimensions: Historiographical debate: was Bindusara primarily a consolidator or expander?
Taranatha's claim of southern conquests vs. lack of corroborating evidence
Comparison with Chandragupta (founder/expander) and Ashoka (Dhamma-based consolidator)
UPSC trap: attributing specific territorial gains to wrong Mauryan ruler

concepts.name: Ptolemaic-Mauryan Contacts During Bindusara's Era
key_dimensions: Dionysius sent as ambassador by Ptolemy II Philadelphus to Bindusara's court
Source: Pliny the Elder mentioning this diplomatic exchange
Significance: multi-directional Hellenistic diplomacy — not just Seleucid contact
UPSC trap: confusing Ptolemaic (Egyptian Greek) ambassador Dionysius with Seleucid ambassador Deimachus

concepts.name: Bindusara in Buddhist Textual Tradition
key_dimensions: Depiction in Divyavadana and Mahavamsa — primarily as father of Ashoka
His mother identified differently across texts (some link to Chandragupta's queen Durdhara)
Buddhist texts' bias: Bindusara less celebrated due to non-Buddhist affiliation
UPSC trap: Buddhist sources are more elaborate on Ashoka, making Bindusara's portrayal incomplete and source-dependent

concepts.name: Chandragupta-Bindusara Transition: Political Continuity and Change
key_dimensions: Chanakya's role in transition — some accounts suggest he served under Bindusara too
Shift from Jain patronage (Chandragupta) to Ajivika patronage (Bindusara)
Maintenance of Arthashastra-based administrative framework under Bindusara
UPSC trap: Chanakya is strongly associated with Chandragupta — his role under Bindusara is debated and minor

concepts.name: Bindusara in Jain Tradition: Rajavalikatha Account
key_dimensions: Jain text Rajavalikatha as a source — reliability and sectarian bias
Bindusara's supposed indifference to Jainism contrasted with Chandragupta's conversion
Jain accounts of Bindusara's death and Ashoka's accession
UPSC trap: Jain sources give Bindusara the name 'Sinhasenha' — different from all other traditions

concepts.name: The 'Sophist' Episode: Intellectual and Diplomatic Significance
key_dimensions: Bindusara's letter to Antiochus I requesting wine, figs, and a philosopher/sophist
Antiochus's reply: goods can be sent but Greek law forbids selling a philosopher
Source: Athenaeus in Deipnosophistae — reliability and context
UPSC angle: reveals Mauryan court's cosmopolitan intellectual curiosity and Hellenistic cultural exchange

concepts.name: Bindusara's Death and Circumstances of Ashoka's Accession
key_dimensions: Approximate date of death: ~272 BCE — interregnum period before Ashoka's formal coronation (~268 BCE)
Four-year gap between Bindusara's death and Ashoka's coronation — significance of this interregnum
Succession war narrative in Buddhist sources vs. lack of epigraphic confirmation
UPSC trap: Ashoka's accession year (272 BCE) vs. coronation year (268 BCE) — frequently confused in options
